title: They didn’t take Saul’s crown.
paragraphs:
They didn’t take Saul’s crown.
He traded it… for approval.
He looked powerful.

Crowned.
Chosen.
Anointed.

But behind the throne…
was a man terrified of losing the crowd.
And here’s the part we don’t want to admit:

You can be called by God…
and still be controlled by people.

You can be anointed…
and still addicted to approval.

You can look strong in public…
while quietly negotiating obedience in private.

Saul didn’t wake up one day and decide,
“I will rebel against God.”
No.

It was slower than that.
More subtle.
More dangerous.
He started editing obedience.

Softening commands.
Delaying conviction.
Justifying compromise.
Why?
Because eyes were watching.
Voices were loud.

And deep inside…
he needed to be seen.
Pride doesn’t always roar.

Sometimes…
it performs.
The moment is recorded in 1 Samuel 15:24:
“I have sinned… for I have transgressed the commandment of the Lord… because I feared the people and obeyed their voice.”
Read that again.

Not I misunderstood.
Not I forgot.
“I feared the people.”
That’s the fracture point.

Saul didn’t just disobey God—
he replaced God’s voice with human approval.
And suddenly this ancient story feels… uncomfortably modern.
Because we do this too.

You know what God is asking you to surrender…
but you delay.

You know what He’s calling you to walk away from…
but you rename it.

You know that conviction burning in your chest…
but you drown it with distractions.
Why?
Because obedience might cost you:

• That relationship
• That image
• That platform
• That applause
And you’re not sure you’re ready to lose it.
So you perform.

Spiritual on the outside.
Negotiating on the inside.
But here’s where it gets even heavier.

When Saul was confronted by the prophet Samuel,
he didn’t run to repentance first.
He ran to reputation.
In 1 Samuel 15:30, Saul says:
“Honor me now before the elders of my people…”
Do you see it?

Even after sin…
he still wanted to look right.
That’s pride at its most dangerous form.

Not loud rebellion—
but polished disobedience.
This is the trap:

Caring more about how you appear before people
than how you stand before God.
And here’s the sobering truth:
God will not compete with your need to be admired.

Some scholars interpret Saul’s downfall not as a sudden collapse, but a progressive drift—
a slow erosion of reverence replaced by self-preservation.
And that’s what makes it terrifying.
Because drift doesn’t feel like rebellion.
It feels like… adjustment.
But partial obedience is still disobedience.
And delayed obedience is still disobedience.
So where does that leave us?
Exposed.
Convicted.

And if we’re honest…
a little like Saul.
But this is where the story shifts.
This is where grace breaks in.

Because where Saul clung to approval…
Jesus let it go.
Jesus Christ did not come to protect His image.
He came to surrender it.
Philippians 2:8 says:
“He humbled Himself by becoming obedient to the point of death—even death on a cross.”

Jesus was misunderstood.
Mocked.
Rejected.
Publicly humiliated.
And still…
He obeyed.

Fully.
Completely.
Without editing the Father’s will.

Where Saul feared people…
Jesus feared God.

Where Saul grasped for honor…
Jesus laid His down.

Where Saul lost the kingdom…
Jesus established an eternal one.
And here’s the Gospel:
The perfect obedience of Jesus covers your compromised obedience.
Let that hit you.

Your half-hearted surrender.
Your delayed obedience.
Your image management.

All of it…
nailed to the cross.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not when you got it right.
Not when you became consistent.
Not when you stopped caring about people’s opinions.
While you were still stuck in it.
That’s grace.
But grace is not permission to stay the same.
It’s power to finally change.
This is your turning point.
Right here.
Right now.
You don’t have to keep performing.
You don’t have to keep pretending.
You don’t have to keep choosing the audience over the altar.
You can repent.

Not just feel bad—
but turn back.
You can surrender.

Not partially—
but fully.
You can finally say:
“God, I choose Your voice… over every other voice.”
Because the truth is—
The crowd didn’t die for you.
Jesus did.
So why are you still living for their approval?
Let this be the moment you break agreement with performance.
Let this be the moment you stop curating obedience.
Let this be the moment you come back to real, raw, surrendered faith.
The question is still echoing:

The audience…
or the altar?
Choose wisely.
One leads to applause that fades.
The other leads to a kingdom that cannot be shaken.
